findings.claim: The model answer says the Tokaj vineyard classes were 'a Rákóczi-era survey formalized by royal decree in 1737'.

The classification was developed separately: Matolai's work around 1720-1730, then the national censuses of 1765 and 1772 that sorted vineyards into first, second and third class. The 1707 Rákóczi-era national certification ranked whole regions, with Tokaj placed as 'First Growth', not individual vineyards.

It gives 1707 as the year when whole lands were ranked in five groups, with Tokaj as First Growth, and it says the 1737 decree declared Tokaj a delimited wine region with borders, not a vineyard ranking. Wikipedia's Tokaji and Tokaj wine region articles agree. They say vineyard classification began in 1730 and was completed by the national censuses of 1765 and 1772, and that a royal decree of 1737 (or 1757) established a closed production district. So the model answer's claim that the classes were "a Rákóczi-era survey formalized by royal decree in 1737" is false. question.q: Compare Xinomavro as it is expressed in Naoussa, Amyndeon and Goumenissa.
accept: naoussa is pure xinomavro and the most structured amyndeon is high cold and sandy goumenissa blends negoska
naoussa full and tannic amyndeon lighter and permitted for rose and sparkling goumenissa softened with negoska
three northern greek pdos for xinomavro with negoska only in the goumenissa blend
same grape three appellations differing by altitude soil and blending partner
question.ans: Naoussa is the benchmark and is monovarietal Xinomavro, grown on the south-east facing slopes of Mount Vermio at roughly 150 to 400 metres - warmer than Amyndeon, and the fullest, most tannic, longest-lived and most classically Nebbiolo-like of the three, all dried tomato, olive and dried flowers over ferocious tannin. Amyndeon sits on the plateau on the other side of Vermio, at roughly 570 to 750 metres, distinctly colder, with sandy soils in which some ungrafted vines survived phylloxera; the wines are paler, higher-toned, more red-fruited and earlier-drinking, and it is the only Greek PDO that permits still and sparkling rosé Xinomavro. Goumenissa, on the slopes of Mount Paiko from about 150 metres up, is the blend: Xinomavro with a minimum 20% Negoska - the familiar 80/20 formula - Negoska being a fleshier, lower-acid, softer-tannin variety that fills the middle palate and rounds the finish. Same grape, three answers - structure in Naoussa, aromatics and lift in Amyndeon, flesh in Goumenissa.
question.exp: Xinomavro's name means 'acid black', and every one of these zones is a different strategy for managing that. If a blind glass shows the Nebbiolo signature with unexpected softness, Goumenissa is the answer the room is waiting for; if it shows the signature at rosé weight, think Amyndeon - the one PDO where sparkling and still rosé Xinomavro are legal, Zitsa (from Debina) being Greece's other sparkling appellation.

findings.claim: The explanation says 'Trebbiano bulks the blend; the Malvasia carries the perfume.'
findings.because: The Frascati DOC rules have changed twice. The 2004 revision (Gazzetta Ufficiale 04A07912) set Malvasia bianca di Candia at 50% or more and capped Trebbiano Toscano at 10-20%. The current rules (last changed 30 Nov 2011, with DM 07.03.2014) require at least 70% Malvasia bianca di Candia and/or Malvasia del Lazio. Trebbiano is now only one of the optional grapes (Bellone, Bombino, Greco, Trebbiano), which together may make up at most 30%. Trebbiano could bulk out the old 1966-era blend, but it has not been able to since 2004, and certainly not since 2011.
findings.fix: Since 2011 Malvasia (di Candia and/or del Lazio) must make up at least 70% of Frascati; Trebbiano is now only an optional grape within the 30% maximum, and the Malvasia del Lazio carries the perfume.

Italian Wine Central gives the same figures and dates the last change to 30 Nov 2011, when Cannellino di Frascati and Frascati Superiore became separate classifications. Under those rules Trebbiano cannot "bulk the blend", so the explanation describes the old blend as if it were current. The question, the model answer and the accept list are fine; only the explanation is wrong. The examiner's fix is right in substance. I rephrased it so it matches the legal text: it names both Trebbianos and all the optional grapes, and dates the rule to the current disciplinare as revised in 2011. I did not open the 2004 Gazzetta Ufficiale text myself, so the fix cites only the rules I confirmed.
findings.finalFix: Under the current disciplinare (revised 2011), Malvasia bianca di Candia and/or Malvasia del Lazio must make up at least 70% of Frascati; Trebbiano (Toscano or Giallo) is now only an optional grape, sharing the remaining 30% at most with Bellone, Bombino Bianco and Greco, and the Malvasia, above all the del Lazio, carries the perfume.
